title: The groupthink trap

audience.who: employees and team leads in corporate teams who run or sit in decision meetings
audience.knows: what it feels like to nod along in a meeting while privately unsure; probably not the name for it or a habit that prevents it
audience.cares_about: not being the one who signed off on an avoidable mistake, and not looking difficult for raising a doubt

outcome: In their next decision meeting, the viewer can notice the moment a team is agreeing too fast and use one simple habit (leader speaks last, everyone writes a view before talking, a named critic, or imagining the plan has already failed) to get the unspoken doubts on the table before the decision is made
through_line: Smart teams agree their way into bad decisions because every doubter thinks they are the only one, so the silence looks like agreement; the fix is not braver people but habits that get each doubt said before anyone commits

arc_plan.what: Framed as invented: one small team, one meeting, one plan. The leader says what she wants first, one colleague agrees quickly, and the viewer can see each other person's private doubt that they never say. The plan passes with every hand up; jump forward in time to it failing on exactly those unsaid doubts. Nobody in the room was foolish.

Name groupthink and where the term comes from, as the knowledge sheet states it. Then the mechanism, in ordinary-meeting terms: the leader's early view sets the direction, early agreement looks unanimous, and each doubter stays quiet because they think they are alone, so silence is read as yes. One plain caveat on how strong the evidence is, as the knowledge sheet words it.

The same meeting replayed with the same people. Three or four habits, each landing on one of the doubts we saw: the leader speaks last, everyone writes a view before discussion, one person is given the critic's job, and the team imagines the plan has already failed and asks why. The hidden doubts come out; the decision changes or gets fixed before it ships.

Pause and predict: a fresh moment in the next meeting where the tempting move is to read silence as agreement; the viewer picks which habit fits before the team shows it. Then the viewer names one decision on their own calendar to try a habit on.
Return to the team, changed: the doubts that sank the first plan now sit on the table, said out loud. The through-line in one breath: the silence was never agreement.

must_cover.what: groupthink named, with where the term comes from, only as the knowledge sheet states it
it is not about stupidity: capable, well-meaning teams fall into it in ordinary meetings
how it starts in an ordinary meeting: the leader's view stated first, early agreement, and doubts held back so that silence is taken as agreement

simple habits that break it, three or four, each as the knowledge sheet describes it (for example: the leader speaks last, independent views before discussion, an assigned critic, imagining the plan has failed)
an honest caveat where the evidence behind the original model is mixed, worded as the knowledge sheet words it
no invented statistics: any number on screen or in narration comes from the knowledge sheet or is framed as hypothetical

must_avoid: statistics, percentages or research findings the knowledge sheet does not state
a lecturing or teacher-like tone, or blaming the viewer for having nodded along
a villain leader: she is reasonable and well-meaning, and the trap is the setup, not a bad person
stereotypes of age, gender, seniority or role in the team
a list of tips in place of habits shown working inside the story
retelling historical case studies as the story; at most a one-line mention if the knowledge sheet supports it
presenting a habit as guaranteed to work
mascots, glow, bouncy cheerleading motion; warm but adult
naming a real company, product or person as the story team
example_posture: One invented, ordinary team of about five, framed with say or imagine, deciding one plain plan (for example, committing to a launch date most of them privately doubt). Same people and same meeting in the opening and the replay, so the change is the only variable. Each doubt is specific and reasonable. No real company, no industry jargon, no drama or raised voices.
visual_direction: A small illustrated story world told by a narrator, not a presenter: one meeting room around one table, outlined characters with readable faces. The viewer sees what the characters cannot: each person's doubt as a private thought, kept hidden. Agreement that visibly accumulates, one nod at a time, until it looks total. Time jumping forward to the consequence, in steps. The replay is the same room with the hidden thoughts turning face up as written notes on the table. The habits as a short set the viewer can carry, returning at practice and payoff. Hand-made feel: motion that steps like drawn frames, shapes that turn into other shapes, scene changes like a page turning or torn paper.
voice_note: A storyteller talking to a colleague, not a trainer: warm, dry, a little wry about meetings everyone has sat in. Present tense for the story, one plain sentence for each lesson, said once. Short; at about two and a half minutes every line has to move the story or the idea.
open_questions: Should the story team have names, or stay unnamed? Left to the script; at most the leader is named.
May the lesson name the historical origin of the term and a case study, or only the term? Depends on what the knowledge sheet can state conservatively.
Length is about 2.5 minutes, so the practice segment is a single pause-and-predict; no second scenario.

look.note: From the request notes: TED-Ed style, a small illustrated story world, one running example team, hand-made feel, warm but adult, never teacherly; a story-cartoon look with stepped, hand-drawn timing, shapes that morph, and a page or torn-paper join; no invented statistics.

inferred: must_cover wording and the four example habits (to be confirmed by the knowledge sheet)
must_avoid beyond the genre and notes
